meta.title: Keeping artefacto current, without ever moving the floor mid-review
meta.goal_md: The page says when a newer artefacto exists and offers one click to fetch it. The review you are in the middle of keeps running the version it started with.
meta.summary_md:
artefacto has no upgrade path. The only way to get a new version is to re-run the install command from the README, and nothing anywhere tells you a new version exists. Someone who installed 0.1.0 yesterday is still running it, still without the skill install that 0.2.0 added.

When this ships, the review page carries a quiet line when a newer release is out, with a button. Pressing it downloads the release for this platform, checks it against the published checksum, runs it once to prove it works on this machine, and renames it over the installed binary. The running server is unaffected — a running process keeps its own open copy of the file — so the review you are watching does not blink. The new version is what runs the next time artefacto starts.

This is revision 2. A critic pass against the live release found revision 1 was not implementable: it downloaded a binary that does not exist, with an HTTPS client the crate does not have, over a file it never defined. All of that is answered below.

The ask: **two blocking questions**. The first decides how artefacto makes an HTTPS request at all — it has never made one, and the four ways to fix that differ by about 3 MB of binary and a whole phase of work. The second decides which file artefacto is allowed to overwrite. A third and fourth question are marked not blocking and can be answered after the command exists.
key_points: **The release manifest is the source of truth, not the GitHub API.** `releases/latest/download/dist-manifest.json` redirects to the current release, is not rate limited, needs no `User-Agent`, and carries the version tag, the artifact name for every target triple, and each artifact's SHA-256 inline. I fetched it and confirmed all of that. Using it removes the API's 60-requests-per-hour-per-IP limit, its 403 on a missing `User-Agent`, and any guessing at asset names.

**The daemon checks, once a day, per machine. No CLI command ever touches the network on its own.** The check runs on the server's existing tick loop and caches its answer in a file shared across every repository, so five checkouts ask once. `artefacto plan push`, `plan check` and `status --json` make no request, ever — only `artefacto update`, which you typed, does.

**Two different questions: how it was installed, and what is installed.** The install receipt cargo-dist writes says *how* and *where*. It does not say *what* — it still reads `0.1.0` on this machine. So the version artefacto compares against the release is read by running the binary at the install path with `--version`, and the receipt is used only to find that path and to prove artefacto is allowed to touch it.

**Replace the file now; the running server keeps its own copy.** Renaming over a path does not touch the process already running from it — it keeps the old inode and its mapped pages. That is a stronger guarantee than deferring the swap, and it is the same reason deferring was safe. It also avoids the macOS code-signature failure that writing in place would cause on Apple Silicon. The rule is **rename, never write in place**, and never restart anything.

**Nothing is applied until it has been run once.** A matching checksum proves the bytes came from the release. It does not prove they run here — a wrong target triple downloads, verifies, extracts, and bricks the install. So the new binary is executed with `--version` before it replaces anything, and must exit 0 and report a version strictly greater than what is installed.
**There is an undo.** The replaced binary is kept beside the new one as `artefacto.previous` and `artefacto update --rollback` puts it back. Two renames in one directory, no copying, no network.

**The no-network claim narrows in the same commit that first breaks it.** The README says artefacto touches no network. That stops being true the moment the first phase merges, so the README changes then — not four phases later.

**Nothing is automatic without consent.** The check is the only thing that happens on its own, `ARTEFACTO_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` turns even that off, and no byte is downloaded until somebody presses the button or types the command.
out_of_scope: Choosing an arbitrary older release: rollback restores the one binary artefacto replaced, and nothing else
Replacing a running server, restarting it, or interrupting an attached agent to apply an update
Updating anything other than the artefacto binary (the skill travels inside it)
Windows support, which artefacto does not have
Updating other repositories' running daemons, which keep the old binary until they next start
Telemetry: the check sends no identifier, no plan content and no repository name (a request does send this machine's IP and a User-Agent, which is unavoidable)

open_questions.question_md:
**How does artefacto speak HTTPS and read a `.tar.xz`?** It has never made an outbound request. All ten dependencies are local: `tiny_http` is a server, `tungstenite` is built with no TLS. And there is no bare-binary asset to download — every release artifact is a `.tar.xz` holding `<target-triple>/artefacto` alongside a README and a LICENSE, so something has to decompress xz, read a tar, and pull one member out.

This is the largest decision in the plan and it changes how much of the plan exists at all. Four real options:

| option | what it costs | what it buys |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) Link a Rust HTTPS client** — `ureq` + `rustls` + a root-certificate source, plus `xz2` and `tar` | ~60-90 transitive crates, roughly 2-4 MB of binary | Self-contained. Testable end to end against a local server. No dependency on what is installed on the machine. |
| **(b) Shell out to `curl` and `tar`** | Adds nothing to the binary. Depends on `curl` existing, and on `tar` reading xz — true on macOS via libarchive, not guaranteed on a minimal Linux image | Tiny. Reuses the exact tool the README already tells people to install. `curl --max-time` gives a real timeout for free, which Rust's `ToSocketAddrs` does not. |
| **(c) Run the release's own installer** — download `artefacto-installer.sh` and run it | Executes a remote shell script. It is not covered by the release's `sha256.sum`, so it cannot be checksummed | Almost the whole plan disappears. I read the published script: it already stages into `mktemp -d` **inside the install directory**, verifies the checksum, and `mv`s over the target — the exact discipline this plan spends a phase reinventing. It is regenerated by cargo-dist every release, so it never goes stale. It also rewrites the receipt correctly. |
| **(d) Use `axoupdater` as a library** — cargo-dist's own updater crate, v0.10.2, published a month ago | Pulls `axoasset`, `miette`, `reqwest`, `self-replace` and their trees — probably heavier than (a) | Purpose-built for exactly this, by the people who generate the installer. Handles platform detection, receipt, extraction and the running-executable replace. |

I would build **(b)**, and fall back to a clear error when `curl` or xz-capable `tar` is missing, telling the person the one command to run instead. It keeps artefacto the small auditable binary the README sells, it makes the timeout honest, and it fails loudly rather than silently on the machines it cannot serve. **(c)** is the tempting one and I would take it if you want this in a day instead of a week — the reason I do not lead with it is that "artefacto downloads and executes a shell script" is a sentence I would rather not have in the README.

Your repository's standing rule is to ask before adding dependencies, which is why this is a question and not a decision.

**Which file is artefacto allowed to overwrite, and when is the answer "none"?**

The shell installer writes a receipt. I read the one on this machine — `~/.config/artefacto/artefacto-receipt.json`, mode 0644 — and it says `install_prefix: /Users/ellery/.cargo`, `install_layout: cargo-home`, `version: 0.1.0`. The install path is `install_prefix + /bin/ + binaries[0]`.

The rule I would build: **artefacto replaces the binary it is itself running from, and only when that path is exactly the path the receipt names.** Both conditions. Canonicalize both sides before comparing, and refuse if the target is a symlink rather than a regular file — renaming over a symlink replaces the link with a file and orphans whatever it pointed at, which is the rule `src/commands/skill.rs` already learned the hard way.

That rule makes three things safe that are otherwise reachable today. A `cargo run` or a `target/debug/artefacto` cannot apply a downloaded release over your own build, or over the real installed copy somewhere else. The test suite, which runs `target/debug/artefacto`, cannot destroy its own build directory. And a second checkout cannot fight with the first.

It also means people who installed some other way — `cargo install --path .`, a package manager, an unpacked tarball — get **no button and no command**, only a line saying a newer version is out and how they installed this one. That is deliberate: the tool that installed it should be the tool that updates it. The alternative is offering the button anyway and replacing whatever is on the `PATH`, which I think is wrong.

What I want from you is whether "no button for those people" is acceptable, or whether it should be no notice at all for them.

**Is a web page the right place for a button that replaces a binary on your machine?**

The page is on loopback, behind a session cookie, a strict `Origin` check and a nonce policy, so nothing else on the machine can reach it. The mechanism is safe. The question is whether it should exist, or whether the page should only *say* a version is out and leave `artefacto update` as the way to do it.

I lean toward the button, because "almost automatic" was the whole ask, and because replacing the file cannot break the review in flight.

**Not blocking**, deliberately. The first two phases build the command and stand on their own without an answer, and this is the question most cheaply answered by shipping `artefacto update` first and seeing whether you ever want a button. Only the `Saying so, and asking` phase waits on it.

**On a machine with no network, or behind a proxy that blocks GitHub, should a failed check say so?**

Silent is quieter, but then somebody behind a corporate proxy never learns that artefacto has been unable to check for a year.

I would follow the precedent `sync_into_agents` already set: say it once, in the server's log, and never in the page. The page is for the review; a failed background check is not something a reviewer should have to read past. **Not blocking** — the answer changes one log line.

risks.title: A new dependency tree, or a new runtime requirement, to make one HTTPS request
risks.mitigation_md: This is `q-transport` and it is the plan's biggest change. artefacto is ten local dependencies and no outbound request; the options are roughly 2-4 MB of linked TLS, or a hard requirement on `curl` and an xz-capable `tar`, or running cargo-dist's own script. No option is free, and the plan does not start `p-fetch` until you pick one. Whatever is picked, `Cargo.toml` is in `t-manifest`'s file list and the README states the requirement plainly.

risks.title: A correctly-checksummed binary for the wrong platform bricking the install
risks.mitigation_md: The reachable case is not corruption, it is target detection. `std::env::consts::ARCH` reports what the *process* is, so artefacto running under Rosetta on Apple Silicon picks `x86_64-apple-darwin`, and that archive downloads, checksums, extracts and passes every criterion before it replaces a working arm64 binary. Same for a glibc build landing on musl. `t-smoke` is the answer: run the new file with `--version`, require exit 0 and a greater version, and only then rename. A file that cannot run is deleted and the old one is never touched.

risks.title: A one-way replacement with no way back
risks.mitigation_md: Revision 1 had none: once the rename happened, the previous binary was unlinked and the only route back was finding an old release URL by hand. Now the replaced file is renamed to `artefacto.previous` in the same directory *before* the new one moves in, so the swap is two renames on one filesystem and the old file survives. `artefacto update --rollback` reverses it. `t-apply` proves both directions, and proves that a failure between the two renames puts the original back.

risks.title: The running daemon keeps serving the old binary's code after the swap
risks.mitigation_md: This is not a bug, it is the safety property — but revision 1 said "the next start is the new version" and meant the wrong process. `plan push` calls `serve()`, which returns immediately when a live server is recorded (`src/commands/serve.rs:33`), and the daemon self-exits only after thirty minutes with no page and no lease. So after a swap the daemon is still old, serving the old `plan.js` and the old routes, and the new CLI is talking to it. `t-server-version` adds a `version` field to `server.json` so the two can tell each other apart, and the page's notice changes to say which version this review is running rather than repeating an offer that is already taken.

risks.title: Silently replacing a newer local build with an older released one
risks.mitigation_md: Reachable on this machine today: the repository is 0.2.0, the binary on `PATH` is 0.1.0, and the receipt says 0.1.0 whatever you do to the binary. Someone who runs `cargo install --path .` from a checkout ahead of the release leaves the receipt untouched and stale. Three rules close it: the version comes from running the install path, never from the receipt; a new binary is applied only when its version is strictly greater than what is installed *right now*, checked immediately before the rename; and the receipt's `version` field is rewritten after a successful swap so it stops lying.

risks.title: `rename` failing across filesystems between the staging directory and the install path
risks.mitigation_md: `std::fs::rename` fails with `EXDEV` across mount points, and `$XDG_STATE_HOME` and `$CARGO_HOME` are independently configurable — this machine's own conventions already redirect cargo output onto an external volume. Revision 1 staged under the state directory and claimed it used "the same staging discipline as the skill install"; it did not. `skill.rs` stages a **sibling of the target** precisely so the rename stays inside one filesystem (`src/commands/skill.rs:330`). So does cargo-dist's installer. This plan does the same: a private directory created inside the install directory, and if even that fails with `EXDEV`, copy — 4 MB is nothing.

risks.title: Staging an executable somewhere another user can write it
risks.mitigation_md: `ambient_base()` (`src/server/state_dir.rs:58`) falls back to `/tmp/.local/state` when `HOME` is unset, and to a relative path when `HOME` is relative. That is tolerable for a review log. It is not tolerable for a file that is about to be renamed onto someone's `PATH` and executed: `/tmp` is world-writable, so a pre-created directory there is enough on any machine running artefacto without `HOME`, which includes some launchd and container contexts. The update paths therefore never use `ambient_base()`. They stage inside the install directory, in a directory this process creates with `create_dir` at 0700, and refuse to apply if that directory is not owned by the current uid or is group- or world-writable. `skill.rs` already refuses a non-absolute `HOME` for the same reason (`src/commands/skill.rs:138`).

risks.title: A tar member escaping the staging directory
risks.mitigation_md: Extraction is where a corrupt or hostile archive does damage: `../` in a member path, an absolute path, a symlink pointing outside, a mode that is not what you expect. The rule is to extract exactly one member — the single regular file whose name is `artefacto` — refuse anything that is not a regular file, refuse any path containing `..` or starting with `/`, write it with `create_new` into a directory this process just made, and set its mode to 0755 explicitly afterwards rather than taking the archive's word for it. `t-extract` has an acceptance criterion for a traversal path.

risks.title: One repository's new binary rewriting the shared skill under another repository's live review
risks.mitigation_md: `sync_into_agents()` runs on every `plan push` (`src/commands/skill.rs:180`) and writes into `~/.claude/skills/` and the other agents' directories, which are shared across every repository on the machine. So updating in repository A means repository B's next push — still on the old daemon — rewrites or is rewritten by a different version's skill text. The rule this implies is already implicit in the code and should be written down: any on-disk format shared across repositories must stay readable and writable by the previous version for at least one version. `src/index.rs:266` already marks the index read-only when a newer artefacto wrote it, and says so once into a log file nobody reads.

risks.title: The README's "there is no network" becoming untrue and staying that way
risks.mitigation_md: It is a claim people choose the tool for. Revision 1 left the fix in the last phase, which would have shipped a false README for three phases. The narrowing now lands in `t-manifest`, the same commit that makes the first request: the review touches no network, and the update check and download are the only things that do.

risks.title: An outbound request hanging a daemon thread
risks.mitigation_md: Replaces revision 1's `r-check-latency`, which described a design the plan did not use — if the daemon checks, `plan push` is never on the critical path and that risk does not exist. The real one is that a daemon making an outbound request is a daemon that can block. The check runs on its own, off the tick thread, bounded by a hard timeout, and every failure collapses to "no answer". `t-check` proves the cached path makes no request at all.

risks.title: Depending on the shape of the release manifest
risks.mitigation_md: Genuinely low only because the plan reads `dist-manifest.json` rather than guessing asset names. Revision 1 rated it low for the wrong reason — it argued a naming change would break the installer first, but cargo-dist regenerates the installer every release, so the installer follows a change automatically and a hardcoded copy inside artefacto would not. Reading the manifest means the names are never hardcoded. A manifest that does not parse is "no answer", not an error.

phases.title: Telling whether this copy is behind
phases.summary_md:
The first slice ships one whole command: `artefacto update --check`. Fetch the manifest, find the artifact for this platform, compare against the binary at the install path, print, exit.

It is deliberately the smallest thing that forces all three of the decisions revision 1 left ambiguous — how artefacto makes a request, which file counts as "installed", and which version is being compared — and it is useful on its own before anything can download or replace anything.

Nothing in this phase writes a byte outside a cache file.

tasks.title: Read the release manifest, and narrow the README in the same commit
tasks.summary_md:
Fetch `https://github.com/elleryfamilia/artefacto/releases/latest/download/dist-manifest.json`, which redirects to the current release. I fetched it while writing this plan; it returns 200 and carries everything needed:

```json
{ "announcement_tag": "v0.2.0",
  "releases": [ { "app_version": "0.2.0", ... } ],
  "artifacts": {
    "artefacto-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.xz": {
      "kind": "executable-zip",
      "target_triples": ["aarch64-apple-darwin"],
      "checksums": { "sha256": "a8b003ea6b4d…" } } } }
```

So the artifact name is looked up by target triple, never constructed, and the SHA-256 is inline — there is no second request for a `.sha256` file, and no need to parse its BSD `<hex> *<name>` format.

Three things this must not do. It must not use `api.github.com`, which is 60 requests per hour per IP and returns 403 to any request without a `User-Agent`. It must follow the 302 to `objects.githubusercontent.com`, and refuse a redirect to a non-HTTPS scheme. And it must send a `User-Agent` naming artefacto and its version, and nothing else.

The README's "there is no network" becomes untrue the moment this merges, so it changes here, not in the last phase.

tasks.title: Which binary is the installed one, and what version is it really
tasks.summary_md:
Two questions the receipt only half answers.

**Where.** `~/.config/artefacto/artefacto-receipt.json` gives `install_prefix` and `binaries`; the path is `install_prefix + /bin/ + binaries[0]`. Canonicalize it. Refuse if it is a symlink rather than a regular file.

**What.** Not the receipt's `version` field — that reads `0.1.0` on this machine and would still read `0.1.0` after artefacto replaced the binary itself. Run the install path with `--version` and parse what it prints. The receipt says *how* it was installed. The binary says *what* is installed.

**Whether artefacto may touch it.** Only when `current_exe()`, canonicalized, is exactly the canonicalized install path. A development build, a copy, a second checkout: no. This is the rule that keeps the test suite from destroying `target/debug/artefacto` and keeps `cargo run` from clobbering a real install, and it is what `q-installed-how` is asking you to confirm.

An install with no receipt reports that it cannot be replaced, and names how it was probably installed, so the page and the command can say something useful instead of nothing.
acceptance: The install path comes from the receipt's `install_prefix` and `binaries[0]`, canonicalized
The installed version comes from running that path with `--version`, never from the receipt's `version` field
A target that is a symlink, not a regular file, reports that it cannot be replaced
A `current_exe()` that is not the install path reports that it cannot be replaced, and says why
An install with no receipt reports that it cannot be replaced, and names the likely install method
Nothing on any of these paths writes a file
validation: cargo test --test update -- installed
a test writes a receipt pointing at a copy of the real binary in a temp directory and runs that copy
a test with the receipt pointing somewhere other than `current_exe()` must refuse

tasks.title: `artefacto update --check`, and the once-a-day cache
tasks.summary_md:
The first shippable thing. Compares the installed version against the manifest's and prints one of three answers: up to date, behind with a version, or cannot tell and why. Exit codes are a contract in this codebase (`src/client.rs:22`), so they are chosen deliberately and documented.

The cache sits in a file shared across every repository — a person with five checkouts asks once a day, not five times. The cached path makes no request at all.

The cache and the staged download do **not** share a root. The cache is harmless and can live under the state base; the staged executable cannot, for the reason in `r-staging-mode`.
acceptance: A first call records the latest version and the time it asked
A second call within 24 hours makes no request and returns the cached answer
A call after 24 hours asks again
The cache is shared across repositories: two different repository roots hit the same file
`--check` prints and stages nothing
The exit codes are documented and distinguish up-to-date, behind, and could-not-tell
validation: cargo test --test update -- check
a test server counts requests and proves the second call makes none
cargo test --test cli -- update_check

tasks.title: Turning the background check off
tasks.summary_md:
`ARTEFACTO_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` stops the automatic check entirely, for a machine that must make no outbound request. Named and documented beside `ARTEFACTO_NO_SKILL_INSTALL` (`src/commands/plan.rs:492`), because they are the same kind of promise.

It stops the *background* check. `artefacto update` run outright still works — the precedent is right there: the automatic thing is suppressible, the thing you typed does what you asked.
acceptance: With it set, no automatic path makes a request
With it set, the page shows no update notice
With it set, `artefacto update` and `--check` still work
It is documented in the same place as `ARTEFACTO_NO_SKILL_INSTALL`
validation: cargo test --test update -- off

phases.title: Getting the new one, and proving it runs
phases.summary_md:
Everything genuinely hard is here: an archive to unpack, an executable to verify, and a file on someone's `PATH` to replace without breaking anything.

The whole sequence is one command invocation with no state left between runs. There is no staged file waiting for the next start, no hook before command dispatch, and no failure that repeats forever — all three were revision 1 hazards and all three are gone.

**Do not start this phase until `q-transport` is answered.**

tasks.title: Download the archive and verify it against the manifest
tasks.summary_md:
Create a private directory **inside the install directory** — `<install dir>/.artefacto-update-<pid>-<random>`, made with `create_dir` (not `create_dir_all`, which would happily reuse one somebody else made) at mode 0700. Staging as a sibling of the target is what keeps the final rename inside one filesystem. cargo-dist's own installer does exactly this (`mktemp -d "$_install_dir/tmp.XXXXXXXXXX"`), and so does `src/commands/skill.rs:330`; revision 1 claimed to copy that discipline while doing the opposite.

Download the `.tar.xz` for this triple into it, SHA-256 the bytes, compare against the manifest's inline `checksums.sha256`. A mismatch, a truncated read or any failure removes the whole directory and reports what happened. Nothing outside that directory is touched.

If creating the directory fails with `EXDEV` or a permission error, fall back to a private directory elsewhere and copy rather than rename at apply time. A 4 MB copy is fine.
acceptance: The staging directory is a sibling of the install target, created by this process at 0700
An existing directory at the staged name is never reused
A download whose SHA-256 matches the manifest is kept
A mismatch or a truncated read removes the whole staging directory and reports it
A staging directory not owned by the current uid, or group- or world-writable, stops the update
Nothing is written under `ambient_base()`

tasks.title: Pull exactly one file out of the archive
tasks.summary_md:
The archive is `<target-triple>/{README.md,LICENSE,artefacto}` — I listed a real one. So this decompresses xz, reads the tar, and takes the single regular file named `artefacto`.

Everything else is refused, not ignored quietly: a member whose path contains `..`, a member with an absolute path, a member that is a symlink or a hard link or anything other than a regular file, and a second member that also matches. The file is written with `create_new` into the directory `t-download` just made, and its mode is set to 0755 explicitly afterwards rather than taken from the archive.

Revision 1 had no task for any of this, which is why its "the download is verified before it is kept" was false — what was verified was an archive, and what would have been executed was a file extracted from it by code that did not exist.
acceptance: Exactly one member is extracted: the regular file named `artefacto`
A member whose path contains `..` or begins with `/` is refused and the update stops
A member that is a symlink, hard link, device or directory is refused
Two members matching `artefacto` is an error, not a last-one-wins
The extracted file's mode is set to 0755 by artefacto, not inherited from the archive
The extracted file is written with `create_new` into the directory this process made

tasks.title: Run it before trusting it
tasks.summary_md:
A matching checksum proves the bytes came from the release. It does not prove they run on this machine.

The reachable failure is not corruption, it is target detection: `std::env::consts::ARCH` reports what the *process* is, so artefacto under Rosetta on Apple Silicon picks the x86_64 archive, which downloads, verifies, extracts, and replaces a working arm64 binary. Every acceptance criterion in revision 1 passed while the install was bricked.

So: execute the staged file with `--version`, with a short timeout. Require exit 0, output that parses as a version, and a version strictly greater than what is installed *right now* — read again at this moment, not at the start of the command, so a newer binary that arrived in between is never overwritten.

A staged file that cannot run is deleted and the old one is not touched.
acceptance: The staged binary is run with `--version` before anything is renamed
A non-zero exit, a timeout, or unparseable output deletes the staged file and leaves the install untouched
A staged version not strictly greater than the installed one is refused
The installed version is re-read immediately before this comparison, not reused from earlier in the command
A binary for the wrong architecture is caught here, not after the swap
validation: cargo test --test update -- smoke
a test stages a script that exits 1, and one that prints nothing, and one that reports an older version; all three must refuse and leave the target byte-identical

tasks.title: Two renames, and a way back
tasks.summary_md:
Rename the installed binary to `artefacto.previous` in the same directory, then rename the staged one into its place, then remove the staging directory and rewrite the receipt's `version` field so it stops lying.

**Rename, never write in place.** A running process keeps the old inode and its mapped pages, so the daemon serving the open review is untouched — that is the property the whole design rests on. On macOS it also avoids the code-signature failure that truncating and rewriting would cause on Apple Silicon.

If the second rename fails, the first is reversed, so the window where there is no binary at the install path is one syscall wide and self-healing.

`artefacto update --rollback` swaps the two back. This is the undo revision 1 did not have: it had nothing, and justified that with an out-of-scope line about downgrading, which was doing work it should not have been doing.
acceptance: The previous binary survives at `artefacto.previous` beside the new one
A failed second rename restores the original at the install path
The receipt's `version` is rewritten to the new version after a successful swap
The staging directory is gone afterwards, on success and on every failure
`--rollback` restores the previous binary and reports which version is now installed

phases.title: Saying so, and asking
phases.summary_md:
The part the reviewer sees. One line in the page when a newer version exists, and one button.

This phase waits on `q-who-presses`, and nothing else does.

tasks.title: Carry the version to the page, and let a new CLI recognise an old daemon
tasks.summary_md:
The page has no way to learn a version today. `state_json` (`src/server/page.rs:376`) does not carry one, `status_json` does not, no event type would deliver one, and nothing in `src/` reads `CARGO_PKG_VERSION` outside `skill.rs`. Revision 1 listed only `plan.js` and `plan.css` for the notice, so its real work was in files it did not name.

So the state payload gains the running server's version and, when the check has an answer, the latest one. Read at page load and on reconnect. A static export has no server, so it gets neither and the notice cannot appear — which is the behaviour the notice wants anyway.

`server.json` gains a `version` field too (`ServerFile` in `src/server/state_dir.rs:18` has `pid`, `port`, `secret`, `started_at` and nothing else). Without it a new CLI cannot tell it is talking to a daemon running older code, which after any swap is the normal case for the next thirty minutes.

files.note: the state payload carries the running version and the latest known one
the daily check runs off the tick loop, not on any command path

acceptance: The state payload carries the running server's version
It carries the latest known version only when the check has an answer
A static export carries neither
`server.json` records the version that wrote it, and an older `server.json` with no version field still parses
No CLI command makes a network call: the check runs only on the daemon's tick loop
validation: cargo test --test server_loop -- state_version
a test proves `plan push`, `plan check` and `status --json` make no outbound request

tasks.title: A notice in the page, in the existing notice component
tasks.summary_md:
A new kind carrying the version that is out and the one running, in a neutral voice — this is the tool talking about itself, not a message from the agent.

Two details in `plan.js` that will bite whoever builds this. `noticeNode` (line 2874) unconditionally calls `agentMark(spec.mark)` and falls back to `agentTitle()` for the kicker, so the agent-free voice is a change to `noticeNode`, not just a new entry in `NOTICE_KINDS` (line 2864). And `renderNotices` (line 2891) iterates a hardcoded list of kinds — a kind missing from that array renders nothing, silently, which looks exactly like a bug somewhere else.

Dismissal has to survive a reload, so it goes in `localStorage` keyed by the dismissed version, following what the page already does for the theme — including the `try`/`catch`, because the static export runs under an opaque origin where touching `localStorage` *throws* (`plan.js:408`, `plan.js:795`).

After a swap the notice does not disappear, because the daemon is still old. It changes: *version X is installed; this review is running Y, and will pick it up when this server next starts* — with nothing to press.
acceptance: The notice appears only when a newer version is known
It names both versions
It carries no agent name, mark or avatar
It does not appear on a static export
Dismissing it survives a reload, and a later version brings it back
Reading `localStorage` under an opaque origin cannot throw out of the render
After a swap it says the review is still on the old version and offers nothing to press
validation: cargo test --test browser -- update_notice
the dismissal test must reload the page, not just assert the node is gone

tasks.title: The button, and what it says while it works
tasks.summary_md:
Pressing it asks the server to download, verify, smoke-test and apply. The notice says it is working, then what happened.

The route is in `src/server/ingress.rs`, as a new `Command` variant — `POST /a/<artifact>/cmd`, behind the page cookie and the strict `Origin` check. **Not** `src/server/verbs.rs`, which revision 1 named: that is the agent's `/cli/` surface behind the bearer secret and the lease session token, which the page does not have and must never have. Revision 1's own acceptance criterion described ingress while its file list said verbs.

One thing ingress does that this must not: every command it handles today is committed to the event log. An update request is not a fact about the review, and logging it means the fold replays it on the next server start. It belongs with `server.stopping` and `nudge` — delivered, never logged. The surrounding code's default is the opposite, so this needs saying out loud and testing.

One request at a time. Pressing twice does not download twice.

files.note: a new `Command` variant; the page's cookie surface, not the agent's bearer one

acceptance: The route is on the page's cookie-and-Origin surface, never the bearer one
The request is delivered and never written to the event log
Restarting the server does not replay the update request
Pressing it applies the new binary and the notice says the review is still on the old one
A failure says what happened and leaves the notice pressable again
Pressing twice does not download twice
An install artefacto may not replace shows no button at all
validation: cargo test --test browser -- update_button
a test restarts the server after a press and proves the fold replays nothing

tasks.title: The spec and the build record
tasks.summary_md:
The README already changed in `t-manifest` and `t-off`, which is the point — it was never allowed to be false in the meantime.

What is left is design, not description. The spec gains four rules as decisions with their reasons: the release manifest rather than the API; rename and never write in place; run it before trusting it; and the rule `r-shared-skill` implies, that any on-disk format shared across repositories stays readable and writable by the previous version for at least one version.

The build record gets the round, including what the critic pass found — that revision 1 downloaded a file that does not exist, with a client the crate does not have, over a file it never defined.
acceptance: The spec says why the manifest is read instead of the API
The spec says rename, never write in place, and why that makes replacing a running binary safe
The spec states the cross-version compatibility rule for shared on-disk formats
No document claims artefacto touches no network
A screenshot of the notice is in the record
validation: the gate: cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy --all-targets, cargo test

tasks.title: The README's update section
tasks.summary_md:
One section covering the four things somebody needs: `artefacto update`, `--check`, `--rollback`, and `ARTEFACTO_NO_UPDATE_CHECK`. Plus the honest narrowing of what "no network" now means, and — depending on `q-transport` — what has to be installed for the update path to work at all.

It also has to say plainly who gets no button: if you installed with `cargo install` or a package manager, artefacto tells you a version is out and leaves updating to the tool that installed it.
acceptance: All four of the command, `--check`, `--rollback` and the off switch are documented
Any runtime requirement `q-transport` introduces is stated, not assumed
It says which installs get no button, and why
validation: cargo test --test cli -- update_help
